utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We shall hear this session in open session. Registrar, can you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is case number IT-03-67-T, the Prosecutor versus Vojislav Seselj. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. Today is Wednesday. I would like to first of all greet the witness that I can see on the screen, Mr. Seselj, Ms. Biersay, Mr. Marcussen, their associates and all the people assisting us. I would like to tell Ms. Biersay that she has had 47 minutes so far and you have one hour and 13 minutes left since you have been granted two hours, and we must not waste any time because Mr. Seselj will have two hours and time is valuable. I shall give you the floor straight away therefore.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will try to use far less of the time that the Court just indicated just so that we can be sure to be finished today.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. I would just like to take a step back to yesterday. Now, we -- close to the end of yesterday we were talking about the April 1st Assembly session. The speech that Mr. Seselj gave in the Assembly as well as the media coverage that followed. Now, after that Assembly session, as you told the Court, Mr. Seselj came to Hrtkovci; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And after you learned about his speech on the 6th of May, you decided very clearly that it was time for you and your family to leave Hrtkovci; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And in order to do that, you took certain steps to obtain official records; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: As you were undertaking those preparations, getting the documents, and I don't want to talk specifically about the documents yet because I will ask that we move into private session to discuss that more in detail, but I wonder if you could describe to the -- the Trial Chamber the general atmosphere as you were trying to get these documents. Was it a calm environment or was it not? Could you describe the atmosphere in which you were trying to get these documents in order to prepare for your departure.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in simplest terms, we were upset by the very fact that we had to take steps that were actually contrary to what we wanted to do. I doubt or at least I don't know --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot hear the witness at all. I heard Madam Biersay very well, but I can't hear the witness at all. Could the witness please say a few words to see if we -- yes, I can hear him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I would say in brief that people were upset. There was fear. There was uncertainty. So that would be it, in briefest terms.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: And, of course, the uncertainty as to the final outcome. The thing that made it easier for us was that we were able to get our documents very quickly, the documents that we needed to cross the border. Many of those who had decided to leave did not have passports or other documents that they had to procure from the authorities. All that was done very quickly. It was like on an assembly line, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'd like to follow up on two things that you said. The first is that you said that you and your family were feeling upset about having to do this because it was contrary to what you wanted to do. Now, what do you mean by contrary to what you wanted to do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I meant was that I didn't actually want to leave my homeland, to put it quite simply.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And the second thing --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wanted to stay there, to stay where I had spent most of my life. That's what I really wanted, but given the circumstances, it appeared that any such wishes were pure delusion. I was quite convinced that given the circumstances, I could not stay there - now I'm talking about myself and my family - without incurring a risk of something untoward happening to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: You also described that many others were also trying to obtain documents. Who -- generally speaking - you don't have to give names - but what type of people were trying to leave Hrtkovci around the time that you were trying to get together these -- these documents to leave Hrtkovci? Were the many others that you talked about --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I take it that you want me to tell you what ethnic group they belonged to, those people who tried to obtain the documents and

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Your Honours, we'd request a redaction for the last sentence, because we believe it may tend to identify the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please prepare a redaction order.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Are you -- are you able -- you said many others. Are you able to estimate -- perhaps you can, perhaps you can't, but are you able to estimate the number of people who -- non-Serbs who were leaving around the time that you were preparing to leave?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, I set off and some of the people I knew had the documents they needed. At the time, the most important document was the passport. And some people, maybe 10 or 15 people that I saw in the Ministry of the Interior premises, the police administration in the municipality of Ruma, did the same thing as I did. They didn't have the documents. When I set off, I was there with about ten people. There were about ten people with me. In that same time period, several dozen people set off.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Before the May 6th speech by the accused, were there non-Serbs who had already left Hrtkovci?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Some had left already, and I know that a couple -- a few of them had left before I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: And maybe two or three families - I can't give you the exact number - had left even before that speech held by Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So just -- just to be clear, approximately -- as far as you know, approximately how many people left before the May 6th speech?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, two or three families. I'm not quite sure about the number left before the speech, but not many at any rate. I know specifically one family that had left, and I heard later that maybe one or two families had left. I don't recall that clearly because a long time has passed, but I know for sure that not many people had left. I didn't have any other information.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So compared to before the -- if we're comparing before the speech, May 6th, and after the speech, when did most of the people -- when did most non-Serbs, as far as you know, start leaving Hrtkovci?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Many more left after the May speech.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: At this time, Your Honours, if we could please go into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'd now like to move to the trips that you began to take between Hrtkovci and Croatia in order to find a house for exchanging purposes. When did you begin going to Croatia to find a house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 13th of May, I set out in two vehicles. There were five of us in those two cars. On the 13th of May, in the morning, and then in the afternoon of that same day, we reached Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I don't want you to say specifically who was in the -- the cars with you, but were your family members with you or other people who were trying to leave Hrtkovci?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was only one distant relative in that group of people. The others were acquaintances.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Were they also non-Serbs who were looking for houses for exchange purposes in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: When you first went on this trip, did you try to have any meetings in order to -- in an effort to help the non-Serbs back in Hrtkovci as far as making their situation known?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I could just say that I did talk with some people or quite a number of people about my own intentions. I wasn't trying to talk anybody into trying or doing the same thing that I was going to do, but I said that I had decided and that it was my sense that we were living in such circumstances where we were not safe and that I believed that it would be good to leave Hrtkovci and to try to move to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: What --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In view of the fact and -- and the nature of my work, I had contacts with a lot of people, so I cannot really remember exactly with how many people I discussed this, but it was definitely a number of people. I primarily talked about my own intentions and decisions.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did you at any time try to inform the media about what was happening in Hrtkovci?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did, but only after I reached Croatia. We tried and we succeeded, I think. We managed to make an appointment to be received at the office of the then president of Croatia, Mr. Tudjman, and we were received at his residence by one of his advisors. We spoke with him about how good it would be to inform the media, primarily the foreign media, and that it would be a good thing and perhaps a blessing for them to appear there and to prevent any possible outbreak of violence. At that time, those few first days in Zagreb, and since the telephone lines were not working properly with Serbia, we found out through Macedonia about the things which later proved to be incorrect, that there was violence raging in the village, that many houses were burned, and then this prompted us to take the steps that I talked about. However, this information proved to be incorrect. There were no houses set on fire. There was more or less some violence, but that could be described as just incursions into homes in the form of a warning, and there was some bombs thrown into yards. I heard that some people had been beaten. I didn't see any of this, but it is something that was discussed at that time. The information that we did get through Macedonia proved to be incorrect. The ones about the burning and the beatings, that was actually not correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Is it fair to say that from May 13th until you finally moved that you were going back and forth between Hrtkovci and Croatia to find a place to live in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: What reports, if any, would you get from your wife when you would go back to Hrtkovci? Did she report anyone coming to the house and asking to move in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is precisely the information I received. There were few visits of people that she didn't know who were persuading her, or you could say even suggesting to her to exchange their homes, which happened to be in different places in Croatia. A number of them, some of them, were quite polite, I would say, and made their suggestions in a civilised and peaceful manner, but she told me that there were also several who behaved in a threatening way. This is what she told me when I came back after my first visit to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did there come a time that someone offered to protect your house 24 hours a day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And could you --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Aleksa Reljic [as interpreted] from the Serbian Renewal Movement visited me at my house and offered to talk, and he offered 24-hour protection for me, my family, and my house. He said that this would be provided by two armed men. There were some others. There was another man, not from Hrtkovci but from Ruma, who suggested that I move to his house with my family and that would be how he could protect me from any possible attacks.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did you feel safe enough with those offers of help to change your mind and stay in Hrtkovci?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. No, I didn't feel safe. Well, I did think that that kind of protection would prove to be a good thing if necessary, but the offers that were made to me, I did not really consider sufficient reason for me to change my decision to leave. Even the armed protection or the relocation that were offered to me, I did not consider that to be something lasting, nor could it be a permanent sort of solution for me.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: On what approximate date did you finally arrange an exchange, a house exchange?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The house exchange was organised in the period from my first visit to Croatia up till the 29th of June, 1992. I don't remember the exact date, it was a long time ago, but all that was necessary from the legal point of view was done in order to be able to make this exchange.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mrs. Biersay, on page 12, line 14, I think the witness said Aleksa Ejic and not Reljic, and so just for the purpose of the record you might wish to clarify this.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, the last name of the person who offered you protection, is the last name Ejic, E-j-i-c?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, I'm not going to -- because of the time issue we have I'm not going to go into the detail of the exchange. I expect that you'll be asked about that later. What I do want to ask you, however, is you had gotten your papers in order for your family; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And eventually you were able to arrange for an exchange of houses, one in Croatia in exchange for the one that you lived in in Hrtkovci; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And your family members also prepared and in fact did leave Hrtkovci with you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: That would include your -- your two parents?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: My parents, my wife, my daughter, and me.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: How old were your parents when you had to leave Hrtkovci?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to work this out. I'm sorry for the pause.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that my father was about 75 or 76, or 73 or 74. I don't want to use too much time on this. And my mother was a couple of years younger. So that was more or less their age.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: May I have one moment, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: At this time, Your Honours, I'm prepared to end my examination here with a respectful request that perhaps ten minutes can be accorded me if we have enough time and if the Court deems appropriate after Mr. Seselj's examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. First of all, I have something to say. I am not in agreement with this demand by Ms. Biersay. It's an impossible demand, because this is a Court witness, and my word has to be final in relation to the Prosecutor. Ms. Biersay cannot have the last word. So this is why I'm first asking you to deny this request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, Chamber witnesses are in a legal situation in which they are in total control by the Trial Chamber. However, the parties, the Prosecutor and yourself, have the possibility to ask them questions under the control of the Judges, obviously. It could be, but that's only an assumption, that one of your questions may lead the Prosecutor to ask another question as this has to do with the collection of evidence or the -- looking for the truth. So it's just an assumption. She said maybe, but we don't know. It will all depend what you are going to say. But even on this assumption, if she ever takes the floor again, the Trial Chamber, from the point of view of fairness, may decide to give her the floor again, and that's why I think that without further ado you may proceed now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I just wanted to check if my procedural rights are still being violated. They are being violated, but I will continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. VS-067, I'm interested primarily why you asked for protection measures. Why are you testifying anonymously in these proceedings? Who is threatening you? Who are you afraid of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I requested protective measures for a simple reason --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Hold on, Mr. Seselj. The Trial Chamber decided that the protective measures which were granted are of a permanent nature and are not to be questioned. So your question should not be put, but if you want to waste your time, that is your problem. In that case, your questions must be put in closed session, but I'm going to confer with my colleagues on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, first of all, the Chamber, after deliberating on this, authorises Mr. Seselj to put questions about the protective measures, but that shall be done in closed session. And the Chamber wants to stress right away that this measure is final regardless of the questions and the answers. So, Registrar, let's move into closed session, and Mr. Seselj can put his questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. No, no, no. Gentlemen, Judges, I did not ask for a lifting of the protective measures. I'm interested in why the witness requested protective measures, because I believe that he's not threatened in any way. If you're asking for these questions to be put in closed session, then I have absolutely no interest in putting these questions to him. I'm not going to put a single question to him that would require going into closed session. I'm not interested in truth in a private session, because this is something that is not accessible to the public, and something that is not accessible to the public cannot constitute truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. We will remain in open session, and you will ask other questions other than the ones regarding protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I give my personal opinion? I think the Defence is entitled to ask these questions in open session to test the credit worthiness of the witness, and the problem of remaining measures is not in question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Hold on. Let me confer with my colleague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the majority of Judges in Trial Chamber, Judge Antonetti and Judge Harhoff, feel that if questions can be put on protective measures, they can be put in closed session, not in open session. There you have it. So, Mr. Seselj, you said that you are going to move on to something else. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You talked about two waves of refugees that appeared in Hrtkovci. In my opinion, and now I'm asking for your opinion on the same, you could not really clearly differentiate between these two waves. In the beginning people came from all different parts of Croatia because it was impossible for them to remain. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And the second --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are right to the extent that people did arrive from all parts of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And people were arriving from those areas where there was no fighting. They were not arriving from the area of the republic of the Serbian -- Serbian Krajina which were under Serbian control. They were coming from Zagreb, Varazdin, Rijeka and other areas where there were no immediate combat activities. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did meet several such people, and they did not come from areas affected by combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Then there was a major exodus of Serbs from Western Slavonia in December 1991. Do you remember that? Western Slavonia fell under Croatian control almost entirely except for Pakrac and a -- other than Okucani and an area around Pakrac; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And then there was a large group of Serbian refugees literally from the front. Many men were in uniform. Some were carrying weapons. Is that whom you were thinking of when you said that refugees were coming with weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: To tell the truth, I don't know if they were arriving from specifically the areas that you are referring to, the ones with arms. It's possible that they were. When I was talking about the first wave of refugees, I was not aware that any of them were -- was in possession of weapons or that any of them behaved violently.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Now, I do allow for the possibility in this second wave in this major exodus from Western Slavonia that some people did have weapons. However, I'm interested in this: When some of them arrived at Hrtkovci and then they were accommodated, some in empty houses because their owners were abroad working; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were a lot of people from Hrtkovci who were working abroad.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Entire families in Germany, Austria, Switzerland, France; is that correct? These are the four countries where they most frequently went.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Their homes were often empty, so when we're talking about forced entry, what we're talking about, first of all, were these empty homes. They are other people's homes, and this does involve interfering in other people's property, but they were already empty.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, it's possible that those houses were empty, some of them, but in most of them other family members such as parents of those people lived in those houses. As far as I know, there were few of those houses that were entirely empty.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes, but we have cases in which the police --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: -- would interfere months later.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I would just ask that there be a pause. Mr. Seselj is speaking before the translation is finished, and it's difficult to follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But on several occasions the police, and I have police records and reports, and I published quite a few of them in a book of mine. I must not mention the title of the book because the transcript would be redacted immediately. I don't know if you've heard about the book. But all the police interventions for the most part had to do with evicting the refugees from empty houses. I'm not aware of a single case in which refugees had moved into a house where somebody was already living, the -- forcibly entered, and then the police threw those people out.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about cases that you are unaware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, I didn't see any such cases mentioned in the two statements that you gave to the Prosecution. Now, tell me this: When the Serb refugees arrived, the second wave, the refugees that carried weapons, some of them, and they found accommodation, some in an empty house. They would move in with their family. Some asked to be allowed to move into a house where there were already people living, to join the household. Some of them were in collective accommodation. So they were all -- accommodation was found for all of them in Hrtkovci; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for some of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And they started living in Hrtkovci in a way; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, as for the weapons that they had brought with them, did they continue carrying them? For instance, they go to a cafe with a rifle slung across their backs? Were there such cases?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether it was those people who carried weapons or not. That's something I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But did you see people carrying weapons just like that, as they walked through the village, rifles?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not rifles. I saw pistols that they carried in their belts.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, yes, you carry a pistol on your belt and one would assume that they had appropriate permits for them. A lot of people in Hrtkovci had permits to carry pistols?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know if they had permits or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes, but if you carry a gun on your belt, you keep it under your coat. I often wear a gun when I'm free, when I'm not in gaol, but I always carrying it concealed under my suit jacket. Did they parade those weapons openly, or were you able to notice from time to time that some people were carrying pistols on their persons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, whether they paraded openly with weapons or not, I'm not sure that you could actually use that term, but I'm absolutely sure about what I saw. I saw some people, a few people, I don't know the exact number, with their weapons tucked inside their belt.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, you could see me in Belgrade carrying a gun in a cafe.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the speakers please speak one at a time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I say in the belt, I meant the kind of belt that is worn by the police and the military, in the holster.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, when somebody carries a pistol in a holster, that is not a threatening way to carry a pistol. The pistol is in the holster, and whoever is authorised to do that can check whether appropriate permits exist. What is important for me is that nobody carried rifles in cafes, on the green market, as they walked around the village. I mean, rifles, automatic rifles, weapons like that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see anyone with a rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I am very happy with your answers. You are a very good witness. You could see somebody with a hunting rifle or a shotgun going hunting. So it's not really horrible if you see a person with a rifle in certain circumstances. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course, if these people are hunters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes, but you're never in a situation to check whether this person is a hunter and whether he carries a rifle because he wants to hunt animals or whether he wants to kill his wife's lover or something like that; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those who carried rifles the way you describe it, I knew them, and I knew for a fact that they were hunters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your answer. Now, the situation in the whole of Serbia was close to the boiling point because of the number of refugees. In April 1992, the official number for refugees in Serbia was 160.000 people. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was a considerable number. Now, as for the figure that you give me, I'm ready to accept it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The appearance of this large number of refugees is a cataclysmic occurrence by its very nature. Am I right? It's akin to a flood or an earthquake. Is that similar to that situation? All of a sudden you have this influx, this flood of 160.000 refugees, and there were in fact many more of them because some never registered. They simply went to live with their families. Are you aware of those cases?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that a large number of people came into Serbia. I know that from the media reports. Now, I don't know the figure and there's no reason for me not to take your figures at face value, and I'm sure that an influx of such a large number of people caused significant problems. I'm sure that it caused great deal of difficulties for the Serbian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You are an intellectual. Let me ask you a question that calls for your expertise. Am I right when I say that when you have a disaster such as an earthquake, a major fire or a flood, do other regulations apply then? Is it possible then? Is it allowed to move into a house that doesn't belong to one in order to find accommodation, and is it not the case that other citizens whose houses are not affected by the disaster to take in those whose houses had been destroyed, because there are such regulations that apply if there's an earthquake or a flood or a major fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I stand because in this one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: -- question, Mr. Seselj has asked three or four questions. And so I wondered if it would be -- if he could break them down into individual questions to assist the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a man who has proven that he is an intellectual, that he's a reasonable man, that he is much more reasonable than the average witness called by the Prosecution, by Madam Biersay, and there is no reason to humiliate him by making me break down the question. I'm sure that he's understood me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So if there's a major earthquake, fire, or flood, is it quite logical? Do these rules not apply in the human community, that people who were affected by it to be accommodated in empty houses and apartments or to be housed -- housed in apartments of those people who were not affected?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In natural disasters that you're talking about, because of solidarity or humanity, it is quite logical and natural for these people to be housed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And the authorities, the local authorities and the authorities at the state level, have to consider the situation and see where it would be most propitious to house those people, because those people cannot just stay outside in the street with their children in the snow and the cold.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's normal for the authorities to do that, and it's also normal for the citizens to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Very well, then. Let us then consider an excerpt from the book that was shown -- authored by me that was shown to you as Exhibit 1062 ter. It is called "The Words of a Member of Parliament." You were able to see this, and you were also able to see the transcript, the original, 1062 ter. It is a broader transcript that shows you that there was a debate in the Assembly about the refugees.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That was on the 1st or on the 2nd of April, 1992; is that right? Well, the date is not important. Do you see from the first part thereof that I actually engaged in a debate with some of the members of the parliament from the Serbian Renewal Movement and the Serbian socialist party and from the democratic party. You can see that from the shorthand record of the session of the Assembly who spoke before I did and who wanted the refugees to be banned from employment, from getting permanent employment, and from buying property in Serbia. Did you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Very well. Then we don't have to read those parts. The Prosecution has seen this, and so has the Trial Chamber because it has been translated into English. So first of all, I have a debate with them, and I oppose their demands to prohibit the refugees from getting employment, and I also oppose their demand that the refugees should be prohibited from buying property in Serbia, and that was gist of the debate.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. According to this text it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And then I engage in a debate with Antun Skenderovic, and in one of the interventions I, in fact, say at page 173 in my book: "If Croats are expelling Serbs en masse in Croatia, what are Croats in Serbia, in Belgrade, waiting an exchange of the population. As many Croats as were expelled by the Serbs -- by the Croats -- by Franjo Tudjman in Croatia should be expelled by Serbs here in Serbia. And that would be the exchange. They can go to Zagreb." Have you been able to read this part? It's at the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So for all intents and purposes, I advocate retortion here as an MP of the opposition. Do you remember how many MPs were there from my party, the Serbian Radical Party, in the Serbian parliament or Assembly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't really recall the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, it was just me. I was the only one. Do you recall now? Did I refresh your memory?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not really, but I have no reason to -- not to trust what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And then Antun Skenderovic stands up. You remember him. He was the president of the Croatian party in Serbia. It's the Democratic Alliance of Croats in Vojvodina or something of that sort, the Democratic Community of Croats in Vojvodina. More or less that was the -- along those lines.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was along those lines and it existed, but I don't recall that gentlemen, so I don't know if it's relevant at all or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And then I answer. Please look at what I'm saying. Mr. Skenderovic should know that under the international law there is the principle of retortion or in Serbian, retaliation. If a state expels members of a national minority from its territory to another state where the majority of those people who suffered that fate live, under international law retaliation can be applied and counter-eviction of the members of the minority in the state where the other parties in the majority can be effected. After all, such exchanges of population are nothing new, globally speaking. After all, if we had grounds to expel I don't know how many hundreds of thousands of Germans for collaboration and for serving the Nazi Germany, Croats have many more reasons to be expelled because Germans could not dream of the kind of crimes that Croats had perpetrators -- perpetrated. You said that this principle of retortion was not humane at all.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, something along those lines. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, I agree with you, but you cannot really say that international law is humane, can you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if there is such a provision in international law, the one about retortion, then it would be my opinion that this law is not humane at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with you. But for instance, the Western powers accuse Serbs of doing reparation [as interpreted] against Albanians in Kosovo. Maybe you think they have cause for that but that's not important. The Western powers say the Serbs threaten Albanians in Kosovo, let's bomb Serbia. 2.500 of civilians in Serbia were killed by way of retaliation. Is that is not retortion? A 3-year-old child was killed in my neighbourhood, Milica Rakic. Is that retaliation? Cruel, inhumane, but it's there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, you are giving an international law lecture to the Judges or to the entire courtroom. This is not a cross-examination what you're doing.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Lattanzi, you have shown that you understand me best and you protected my procedural rights. I'm not lecturing anyone. This witness spoke about the fact that the retaliation is inhumane. I agree with him, but the fact that retaliation is inhumane does not mean that it does not apply under international law.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Have you read anything by Pearl Buck, an American writer? She wrote about 20 novels.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you asking me? No, I haven't read any.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Twenty of her novels have been published in Serbian. In one of her novels she describes what the Americans did in World War II. She devoted a whole novel to that. The Americans took all the citizens of Japanese descent and interned them for preventative reasons. We know a lot about Hitler's concentration camps. We know less about American concentration camps. They put all of their citizens of Japanese descent in concentration camps during the Second World War as a preventative measure. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, in Serbia nobody put members of the ethnic minorities in concentration camps during the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, I read Pearl Buck when I was young, like everyone did. I'm surprised to see that the Americans threw Japanese into gaols. Weren't these administrative retention camps? Are you sure that the word "concentration camp" was used?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, please, what's the difference between a collection centre and a concentration camp where you have guards and you're surrounded by barbed wire in both cases?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The difference is huge, but we will not spend time on this. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the Ustashas had this infamous camp, Jasenovac, in which 700.000 Serbs and 60.000 Jews and 35.000 Roma were killed. They call it a collection camp, not a concentration camp. So terms are merely used to hide the real nature of things. That's what words are used for.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So now the key sentence that I say by way of conclusion of my debate with Skenderovic, and I say what Madam Biersay tried to gloss over yesterday. And let us not forget, Mr. Skenderovic, the current regime in Serbia is too lenient towards you. So I'm criticising Milosevic's regime as being too lenient. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you could say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: After the next or some other elections when the power in Serbia is changed, there will be no forgiveness. Pursuant to that same law according to which Tudjman expelled Serbs from Croatia, we're going to expel Croats from Serbia, and we're not going to allow like the Croats are doing in -- the Croats are doing in Slankamen where they're offering their old, dilapidated houses to Serbs in exchange for their wonderful houses on the Adriatic coast as exchange. The Croats in Slankamen, Zemun and other places will not sleep peacefully until they move because Serb refugees from Zagreb, Rijeka and Varazdin must be found homes. They must be given roofs over their heads, and they must be compensated for the damage they sustained when they were expelled from their homes. Is it clear to you that I am here representing the position of the opposition that would shortly come to power, and I'm publicly stating what the opposition would do once they assume power. Is this clear to you as an intellectual? There is no doubt, isn't there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there is no doubt about what you are saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Very well. There is no need to go into that any longer. Some things are repeated. And you saw at the end, on the 7th of April, that the president of the National Assembly, Aleksandar Bakocevic, distanced himself from my debate and he said that that was not the general position. Did you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm just looking at that now. This is under the heading "President."

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes. He quotes an excerpt from what I said and distances himself from that. I don't want to stay on that too long. If you've seen that, then we can move to something else.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you can move to something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. In relation to this meeting or rally in Hrtkovci which you did not attend; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So you didn't hear all the things that I talked about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In a number of my books I published this address from the Hrtkovci rally. The last time in a book whose title I cannot tell you, but the book is very popular among the Serb public. It has been promoted in all the municipalities in Serbia, and more than 10.000 copies were downloaded from the internet, and I was sentenced to 15 years [as interpreted] in gaol for that book here, but I'm proud of that. I have spent a lot of time in gaol. I was arrested by various regimes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That was something that was written about in the Serbian media.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And you remember that I was proud of every single gaol.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, there might be a mistake on the record. You said you were convicted and you received a 15-months' prison term. I believe it was 15 months, not 15 years.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it seems to me that it was 15 months, but you never know here. 15 months easily turns into 15 years here. But it doesn't matter to me, 15 months or 15 years, it's all the same to me, but it's all right for this error to be corrected in the transcript. I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. On page 151 in that book -- actually, somewhere from page 149 to page 155, I publish this Hrtkovci speech in its entirety. We had the opportunity to see that often here. So this was a programme speech which I gave during an election campaign for the first federal elections in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Do you remember that election campaign for the federal elections?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I don't remember, but I don't have any reason to remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I'm going to remind you. On the 27th of April, 1992, after the Western powers recognised the independence of Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, and Macedonia, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was proclaimed consisting of Serbia and Montenegro; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And a constitution was adopted of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and elections were scheduled for late May 1992. Have I reminded you of the events now?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you have.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In that speech, which was of a policy or a programme nature, I state numerous things that have to do with the political situation. I mostly deal with the political competition, and in one part of the speech I refer to our intentions in relation to the members of the Croatian ethnic minority. Now I'm going to read to you that part of the speech, and this is what I say. This is on page 151 so that the Prosecution can find their place. If Tudjman expelled more than 200.000 Serbs, one part of them is going to come back to the area of the Serbian Krajina, but a part cannot find accommodation there. We have to provide a roof over their heads to those Serbs, and we have to feed those hungry mouths. We don't have money to build new buildings and homes. We don't have the possibility of creating new jobs for them. All right, then. If we don't have that opportunity, then each refugee Serbian family should be given the address of one Croatian family. And then the police, what will they do? The police will do as the authorities decide, and we are going to be in power soon. So all the refugee Serbian families, will come, will come, and knock on Croatian doors and give those Croats their addresses in Zagreb and other places. Yes, yes, they will. There will be plenty of buses. We will take them to the border of the Serbian lands from where they can proceed on foot unless they leave of their own accord. And then I'm talking about some traitors of the Serbian people and so on and so forth. I'm referring to some of those parties and so on, but this is not of importance in these proceedings. Isn't it clear from this passage that as part of the election campaign and making a promise about something that we will do when we come to power. I understand that you don't like this. You are against this from the bottom of your heart, but I'm asking you as a man, as an intellectual, isn't it clear from this that I am promising what we will do once we gain power? I am not moving into action to put this into force before we have come to power. Isn't that clear from what I have read?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, from what you have read that is clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Some people told you that I read a list of persons that should be expelled from Hrtkovci; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I mentioned that this was something that I was told. Given the fact that I did not attend your rally, I just said what others told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Have you heard of Milan Zilic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, listen carefully to what I'm saying, because it's important for the Judges and for the Prosecutor also and for the Defence. That goes without saying. Mr. Seselj is the subject of an indictment based on a number of elements, one of which is a speech he purportedly gave in Hrtkovci on the 6th of May, 1992. Mr. Seselj then reproduces a speech in his book, speech which he gave before the Serbian Assembly session, before the parliament. After having read this, it seems that he stated as follows: If the Serbs are expelled from Croatia, these people need to be welcomed and asks these Serbs to be welcomed by Croatian families. Serbian families should go to the police stations which will tell them which Croatian flats they must go to. At the time, he says that, he is not in power since this is part of a future political platform of his. You seem to be a well-educated man. You seem to be aware of a lot of things. The words of Mr. Seselj at the time, were these conveyed to you in the manner he has just exposed to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I heard it the way it was just said. And from what I understand of the whole matter, what is in dispute is that Mr. Seselj, here in this attempt to present the whole thing, is using the word "if and when they come to power," meaning Mr. Seselj and his party. When they come to power, then this would be implemented, what follows in the text. And according to the positions stated here, it sounds like a platform, a political programme that would be implemented when Mr. Seselj comes to power. I think that Mr. Seselj formulated this question in such a way so as to emphasise that fact, if ever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. I think we're going to take the break. It's 10.30.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President. Mr. President, just a couple of seconds. I would like to ask the witness, because he has already been given or will be given nine documents that I have given to be photocopied. Perhaps he can go over the documents during the break. He doesn't have to read everything. I marked some things also for the Prosecutor and the Trial Chamber. I am also expecting some 20 pages to be given to me of the transcript of the conversation of my team with Ostoja Sibinic and so I would like to have that copied. We're not going to use the entire document, only certain sentences from those documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, let me express again my caveat here, as always, regarding the presentation of such documents. There is no need for me to repeat the reasons why. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, I see on the documents that there is one which arrived on the 16th of February at 13.54 hours, i.e., yesterday. You know that the witness, I'm not going to repeat his -- say his name, was due to come, but you've known that for a long time. So why do you at the last minute ask for this type of document? They have not been translated. Well, obviously the witness knows your language and will have no problem understanding it, but to really convey your system of defence. You know, if we had had that document translated either into English or French, we would have been much more efficient in our understanding of the document, and that's why Mrs. Biersay has risen, to say that she doesn't have the document in her language either. Isn't that right, Mrs. Biersay?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: That's correct. And what is also very concerning is now we will discuss documents that we're unable to read, and we're putting them to a witness who has protective measures, and we have absolutely no idea what's in them. So I would propose that if we discuss any of them, that we do so in closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mrs. Biersay, however, you do have an advantage over the Judges, i.e., you have people with you who work in B/C/S, and during the break maybe we can check that with these people, which I cannot do because we do not have somebody available who can help us at the last minute, but you do have such a person, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, to the extent that we have a break, it should not be considered a working hour or opportunity for the Prosecution. We, too, like Mr. Seselj, are entitled to a break, and it is not conceivable that we can possibly go through with any substantive eye over these documents. It is just not possible. This is about ambush, and Mr. Seselj is a master at it, and we object to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. Your objection is on the record. We're going to take a 20-minute break. Mr. Seselj --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, I agree with Ms. Biersay in one thing. I am the greatest master here at The Hague Tribunal, and the Prosecution has been aware of that for a while now, and that's why they cannot get the upper hand with me. I have these papers, documents, in order to be able to put some questions. I'm not going to tender these documents, and I'm going to be very careful not to uncover or reveal the identity of this witness. This is all that you can expect from me. You have to keep in mind continuously the fact that I am alone here in The Hague. Had I had a regular trial I would have three advisors, a case manager, a rented flat or apartment in the house or in The Hague, and I could just be issuing orders, "Please submit this to the Trial Chamber. Please submit this to the Prosecutor." I cannot do everything myself. This is a vast number of administrative work. Ten Prosecutors have changed here, and can you imagine how many people they have to back them up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, in light of the time it takes to have translations done, the Chamber has made a decision restoring the possibility for Mr. Krasic and Mr. Jerkovic to assist you, and has asked in its decision that their expenses be covered by the Registry as being part of the expenses for the defence of the accused. Now, regarding Mr. Jerkovic, my understanding according to press articles is that he's no longer with you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Slavko Jerkovic left my team as of the 29th of January. He didn't tell me the reasons why he left. We didn't have any contact after that. But the reason is evident. I haven't paid him for a full seven years. I didn't have anything to pay him with. He's a professional lawyer, and he must make a living. So I understand him absolutely for leaving. I don't know what the press is writing. The only time I receive of any news or papers is when my wife comes to visit me, so I don't know what has been written in the press. But Slavko Jerkovic is no longer a member of my Defence team. All I have left now is Mr. Zoran Krasic who has been forbidden to have confidential communication with me, Aleksic and Marina Raguz as case manager, but they're not able to be with me in The Hague and very infrequently visit me. Zoran Krasic has not been able to come and see me for a year and a half. The last time he was here they placed us in a gas chamber and were recording our conversation by a video camera the whole time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In any event, Mr. Krasic can come back to see you. This is part of the decision. So please refer to our decision and read it. So let's now take a break, a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're back in session. I'm going to read the provisions of the decision regarding Mr. Krasic and Mr. Jerkovic so as to try and correct a slight mistake. In the system, here is what it says: "The Chamber authorises Mr. Zoran Krasic and Slavko Jerkovic to assist the accused in public session in the face of presentation of evidence, exculpatory [as interpreted] evidence, in the case -- if this presentation were to be made." So Mr. Krasic may assist Mr. Seselj, but at the time when exculpatory evidence is presented. Should the case arise because as you know there are several options and several procedural possibilities. That being said, and secondly, regarding the question of non-translated documents. The Chamber obviously does not have the translation of these documents and it could be that some confidential information is included regarding protected witnesses. We don't know anything about that, and we do not want to be surprised by the mention of documents which would infringe on our decision either made here in this Trial Chamber or made in other Trial Chambers. So the accused may refer to this document as it was said that it would not be admitted. The accused can say, I have a document saying this and that, et cetera. And I think that the witness has received the documents by fax, so he can see the document in his language. But this document shall not be put on the screen for the sake of protecting potentially protected witnesses. So you may use the document, but you are instructed not to refer to anything that could infer the identification of protected witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry, without referring to the problems I have with the use of this document, I would like to say that my position, as the accused, the Defence, and the Judges know, is slightly different from the one which was just mentioned by the Presiding Judge. So I'm not going to refer back to the whole matter. I just wish to ask again this question which I have already asked, and I wish to stress my reservations about the presentation of these documents and the ways to doing it and the procedure that is followed, as I see it, is not the right one if these documents are presented by the accused. That's all. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Just for the record, I go back to the Presiding Judge's reading out of the decision which we have rendered on the authorisation to Mr. Krasic and Jerkovic, because there is a slight error in the translation. The transcript shows on page 38, line 3, that Mr. Krasic and Mr. Jerkovic will be authorised to assist the accused in public sessions during the presentation of evidence, and then it says "exculpatory evidence." This is a misstatement of the contents of the decision, because the idea was to allow these two associates of Mr. Seselj to be present in public hearings during the Defence case, and that is different. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I say something? Does that mean that they cannot attend the secret sessions or hearings?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: We don't have secret sessions, but we have sessions in -- we have closed sessions, and you are right in stating that Mr. Krasic and Mr. Jerkovic shall not be given access to those sessions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, then they will have no access at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I was just going to ask for clarification of one point with respect to the order. I think it is self-evident from what has been said, but is our understanding correct that the privileged communication of Krasic and Jerkovic have not been restored?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: So, Your Honours, if -- this is something that we may have to come back to, because otherwise the communication between the accused and these two people is subject to monitoring by the Registry so I don't know how this would function in practice but it's something that I guess we will come back to if -- if we get to a Defence case and they will be present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: The issue of monitoring --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm for sure --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: The issue of monitoring is for the Registrar to deal with, and what the Chamber has done is to try and be of assistance in ensuring that Mr. Seselj could benefit from the presence of Mr. Krasic and Jerkovic during public sessions in his Defence case, because we understood that there was also a financial problem in that they were unable to pay for their travel, and this is where the Chamber has wished to extend its assistance to Mr. Seselj's Defence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I can see that you've really assisted me well so that I would be able to look at them as if they were some 25-year-old pretty girls and so that I should enjoy it. Well, once I become a total moron, then it will become possible, and I am not there yet. I am not even remotely on the road to becoming a total moron, although you're trying to turn me into one for seven years, but that's immaterial. Should I continue with my cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed. You've already used up 25 minutes, and you have one hour and 34 minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I asked if you were familiar with the name Milan Zilic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: And my answer to you was that I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: He was the president of the steering committee for the establishment of the Serbian Radical Party in Hrtkovci, and he actually made introductory remarks on the our rally there. So if you were unaware of his name, you were unaware of the existence of the steering committee. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: He was the only person who mentioned any names at the rally. He mentioned the names of the people who had already left Hrtkovci and some of them were members of the Croatian National Guard Corps. That's what he said specifically in his speech and I have his speech here in this book. You didn't hear that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You thought that he read out the names of the people who are supposed to be evicted and expelled, or that I did so.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, more or less that would be the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Fair enough. You said that you were aware of only three families that had left Hrtkovci having first exchanged their property before the rally, three or four families. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, two or three, but it's immaterial.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Fair enough. At page 120 of my book I quote a report by Natasa Kandic from December 1993. It's at page 120. You don't have that but the Prosecution has it. It's the third paragraph marked with number 2. By the 1st of May, 1992 --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Excuse me. Mr. Seselj is referring to one page in a very large book. I asked him yesterday which pages he planned on using. He toll me all 1.000 of them. So we do not have a complete translation of this book, and I don't know if the Court does, but the Prosecution does not. So I'd like to correct that for the record.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judges, I was convicted and sentenced to 15 months in prison because of this book and nobody here at the Tribunal has a full translation of this book yet. I was convicted because of the way I look, not because they read the book. Nobody has read this book. This is a shame for this book. I don't care that you haven't translated it. You received it three years ago. It's your problem entirely. I handed it to you personally here in court, yet you don't want to translate it. Well, I'll translate it. You will have to wait for my translation, but I'll do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So Natasa Kandic says -- it's a very short quote here. By the 1st of May, 1992, around 40 Croatian families had moved out for family reasons and because of their views on the war in Croatia. Some of the families sold their property and some exchanged their property with the Serbs from certain areas in Croatia. So you say three families, Natasa Kandic says 40 families. 40 families times the average of four members per family, that would be about 160 members. So could that be the case?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could be.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I don't want to argue with Natasa Kandic here, whether she says the truth here or not, but all too many -- too many times she doesn't, so it's hard to trust her even when she does.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, can I ask you one thing? In this quote from Natasa Kandic, does -- is it specified what time period she's talking about, when those families moved out?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That's by the 1st of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: But when did it begin?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, when Tudjman won the elections in 1991. I don't know. But the time period is until the 1st of May.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, until the 1st of May. If it's -- if it covers approximately one year, as you've indicated, then I can tell you that this information is completely inaccurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You stated here to Ostoja Sibincic was a member of the Serbian Radical Party and then you corrected yourself when the Presiding Judge warned you that in a report produced by the State Security Service tendered by the Prosecution it is indicated that he was a member of the Serbian Renewal Movement. So you're not sure anymore that he is a member -- that he was a member of the Serbian Radical Party?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you listened carefully to what I said, I said that I thought he was a member of the Serbian Radical Party and that was not a statement of fact on my part.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes, but you state that as a fact in your statement, the statements that you signed, the statements that the Prosecution wrote for you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but, Mr. Seselj, if you followed closely what I had said yesterday, I said that he -- I thought that he was a member of the Serbian Radical Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You said --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I did not ask Mr. Sibincic whether he was a member of the Serbian Radical Party or any other party.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes, but when the Judge asked you how many parties there were in Hrtkovci, you said the Serbian Renewal Movement, the Socialist Party, and the Serbian Radical Party; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Something along those lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And you failed to mention the Democratic Alliance of the Croats of Vojvodina or whatever it was called, and they had a much stronger committee in Hrtkovci than the SPO or the Socialist Party, because this Croatian party, the Croatian party representing the Croatian minority had its branch in Hrtkovci. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, I don't know anything about that, and if there was such a branch or -- of the party I was not a member.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I'm not accusing you of being a member. And even if you were a member, that's not a problem. You have an absolute right to be a member of any party.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't see that as an accusation. I see that as a statement of fact. But I really don't know anything about that party.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The speakers are kindly asked to speak one at a time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you are claiming that and if you have arguments to corroborate those claims, I cannot contradict you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj and Mr. Witness, again we get remarks from the interpreters that they are unable to follow you if you overlap. So please, both of you, observe a short pause between questions and answers. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Could you please look at the papers that you have been given during the break. Document marked with the Roman numeral X.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: It's a transcript of an interview with Ostoja Sibincic conducted by the members of the team assisting me with my defence. Can you see that document.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment. I'm looking for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: It's the last one that you got. It has 60 pages.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have that document in front of me, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes, and --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And neither does the -- neither does the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now the Registrar has told me you don't have it. Then I'll leave it aside for later. I can see the Registrar is now distributing this document to the Trial Chamber. Well, you will receive it. It doesn't matter. Let us go back to that document later. But now, could you please look at those documents that -- as they are arranged, from number 1 onwards. The first document is a transcript of an interview with Dragan Krekic conducted by the team assisting in my defence. Do you know Dragan Krekic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew the Krekic family.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Very well. Here -- well, what is his ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know exactly, but I assume that he -- I assume that he's a Croat, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, he could be a Serb of Roman Catholic faith.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he might.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But at any rate, he is a Roman Catholic. That's not controversial, is it not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I really don't know what his religious affiliation is. I could only perhaps read it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: It's a very -- it's an ample document, so we won't be going through all of it. Could you please look at page 6. He attended the rally, my rally.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have page 6 here with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You have a portion of the text marked, and members of my team ask him whether he saw any armed people in the village, bearded Chetniks with bandoliers, automatic rifles and so on, and he says, Well, they were not wearing bandoliers, but there were people with beards and cockades, and he denies that there were any people with rifles. They may have had their sidearms, pistols, but you could not see that. I don't know. And then the question is whether there were any carrying swords, and he says, "No, I didn't see any." Did you hear any reports that armed persons were present at the rally?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can only confirm that I heard that there had been armed people there. I was told that they were members of your personal guard or escort.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, did they openly wave their weapons or was it just assumed that they were armed because they were my escorts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I heard, those people who were your escort carried weapons visibly. So I say again, this is what I was told. Now, whether this is true or not, I was not at the rally, and I was not an eyewitness. I cannot say it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Fair enough. Did you hear that at that rally I said that all the children from mixed marriages should be killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Nobody told me that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: There was a witness here who testified under oath and with protective measures who claimed that he personally heard at that rally that I said that all children from mixed marriages should be killed. You didn't hear that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I received information as to what you had said there, nobody ever told me anything of the sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Let us look at the next document. It's a statement by Slavko Kulundzic. Do you know him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: He worked in the State Security Service.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And as a member of the State Security Service he was in charge of Hrtkovci. He went to Hrtkovci quite often, did he not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And for the most part, the people in Hrtkovci knew that he was working for the State Security Service, although it's supposed to be a secret.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I knew that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Could you please remove the papers because of the microphone.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Well, I knew that he worked in the police, and now whether everybody else knew, they probably did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You can see the marked parts of his statement. It says that -- well, he claims that there were no armed people at the rally, that there were some people wearing cockades and Serbian traditional caps and fur caps, but that he didn't see any weapons. That's the penultimate and the last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On what page?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: On page 1.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: He says none of the members -- none of the people that attended the rally was armed, and nobody carried bandoliers and rifles, that's for sure.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-067 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: At page 2 he says, some ten days later -- it's the middle paragraph that's been marked here.
